entry.title: Updates from parental leave
entry.content:
Since May, I have been on parental leave, caring for our first child, who was born in September 2025. Making sure the kid doesn’t do anything too stupid will remain my main work responsibility until January 2026, when the responsibility will switch to daycare personnel during working hours.

While parental leave has slowed my research progress, it hasn’t stopped it. In July, I returned to work in order to travel to Portugal to attend the Federated Logic Conference (FLoC). I mostly visited the SAT and CP conferences. The highlight of the trip was being honored with the Early Career Researcher Award by the Association for Constraint Programming.

Photo credits: Dominik Schreiber (left), Katalin Fazekas (middle), and Emir Demirovic (right)

This autumn’s research highlights so far included my PhD student Christoph Jabs defending his dissertation in September and my other student, Antton Kasslin, getting his first two papers accepted. Antton has been working on constraint-based methods for two data analysis problems: scheduling high-school classes with student preferences (paper to be presented at ALENEX-2027, and flow allocation problems that seek to even out the wastewater arriving at a water treatment plant (paper accepted in the Annals of Operations Research journal). In both cases, the work contributes not only a constraint model for the problem, but also new real-world datasets for experimentation and for community use. I am very happy with both papers and with getting to know new communities and research areas. I will make both papers available here once publication is finalized. I want to thank both Antton and representatives at both Helsinki Region Environmental Services and Kyrkslätts Gymnasium for the datasets. I would also like to congratulate Christoph on his well-deserved PhD and his excellent defense.

I will return to full-time work in February 2027.
entry.summary: ...slowing down, but not stopping the research

entry.title: 2026 ACP Early Career Researcher Award
entry.content:
I am very happy to let you know that the Association of Constraint Programming has awarded me the 2026 Early Career Researcher Award. The ACP Early Career Researcher Award is given every year to a researcher who has completed their PhD at most 8 years ago, with a scientific track record showing great promise in Constraint Programming. This year the honor fell to me.

I want to thank the ACP and the CP community for the honor, and also the people who nominated me. I look forward ot being an active member of the community for many years to come.
entry.summary: From the Association for Constraint Programming

entry.title: Best Student Paper at CPAIOR 2026
entry.content:
Since May, I have been on parental leave, which has somewhat limited the time I have to write blog posts. I am, however, very happy to announce that my student Christoph Jabs was awarded the Best Student Paper Award at CPAIOR 2026 for our work “Multi-objective Maximum Satisfiability by Single-Objective Implicit Hitting Set Optimization”.

The paper describes an extension of the so-called implicit hitting set search paradigm to multiobjective optimization. It is the final paper in Christoph’s PhD thesis, and I am happy he could end his PhD work with a nice recognition from the community.

I’d like to thank Christoph and the other coauthors for their work.

entry.title: Uni Junior - Making a game AI with a matchboxes

link.title: Uni Junior - Making a game AI with a matchboxes

entry.content:
After a few years’ break, I organized a workshop as part of the Uni Junior project, which I’ve been involved with for many years now. This time, the workshop focused on game AIs. Specifically, we looked at the (very simple) game of Hexapawn and two different ways to build an AI for it. One of the AIs was rule-based and required its “developer” to specify an explicit rule for which move the AI should make in any given position. The second was a “training AI” that stored good moves in a set of 24 matchboxes and could be trained by removing moves that led to a defeat.

Hexapawn is a tiny, beginner-friendly strategy game played on a 3×3 board using just pawns. Each player tries to reach the opponent’s back row, capture all opposing pawns, or leave the opponent with no legal moves. Because the game is so small, it’s perfect for exploring basic ideas in game strategy and AI, even if even the younger participants of the workshop managed to find perfect strategies for their AIs.

Photos by Stella Saaresaho, the coordinator of Uni Junior.

Thank you to everyone involved in the organization—especially my great assistants, who were fantastic at working with the kids! The Swedish material I made for the lab can (at least for a while) be found on my Google Drive. The idea for the lab was heavily influenced by a YouTube video by Vsauce2 and the AI Unplugged.org materials.

entry.title: AAAI 2026 in Singapore
entry.content:
At the end of January I visited Singapore for the first time in order to attend AAAI 2026. I had two accepted papers, I was there to present a poster on our paper on detecting ordered objectives in MaxSAT and to support my co-author who gave an oral presentation on our paper on efficient and reliable hitting set computations. Additionally, I was invited to give a talk in a workshop on automated reasoning at Nanyang Technological University. There I talked about my more recent work on computing explanations for tree ensembles. I would like thank Yonk Kiam Tan for the invite.

It was my first time visiting both Singapore and AAAI. I am happy with the visit, even if coordinating a conference as large as AAAI has gotten is challening at best. Thanks to the organizers of AAAI and to all colleagues I met in Singapore for the discussions. See you all next time!

entry.title: Papers Accepted at AAAI 2026
entry.content:
I am glad to report that my papers “Ordered Objectives in Maximum Satisfiability”, and “Efficient and Reliable Hitting-Set Computations for the Implicit Hitting Set Approach” were accepted at AAAI 2026 as two of the roughly 4000 papers. Both papers deal with fundamental approaches to combinatorial optimization and how to improve our understanding, efectivenesss and trustworthiness of fundamental AI methods.

I would like to thank all of my coauthors for their work. Once the papers are officially published, I will add links to them on these pages. Before that, you can come to Singapore and talk to us at the posters. See you there!

entry.title: The SAT 2025 Conference
entry.content:
The SAT 2025 conference was organized at the university of Glasgow between the 10th and 15th of August together with CP 2025, and SoCS 2025. These conferences are the most central ones in my field with just under 300 people attending in total. For me it was a busy week, with in total 4 papers with my name on them being presented, and me acting as PC chair for SAT. I learned a lot about the inner workings of a conference, but also had a lot of fun meeting up with international colleagues. I also had the opportunity to meet up with an old high-school friend who nowadays works at the same university, and even see the Beth Mays one-woman show at the Edinbrugh fringe.

I would like to (once again) thank everyone involved in the organization of the conferences. Glasgow and the University of Glasgow were wonderful hosts and I recommend both Glasgow, and Beth Mays show wholeheartedly to anyone.

My student Hannes won the best student paper award at CP 2025
entry.summary: also, the first time I was a PC chair

entry.title: Paper Accepted in Jelia
entry.content:
I am happy to let you know that our paper Engineering and Evaluating Multi-objective Pseudo-Boolean Optimizers has been accepted for publication at the 19th edition of the European Conference on Logics in Artificial Intelligence. In the paper, we report on a cross-community evaluation of different approaches for computing pareto-optimal solutions under 0-1 integer linear inequalities. We also build on out recent TACAS paper in order to show how such solvers can be proof-logged.

I want to thank all of my co-authors, especially my student Christoph Jabs, for their excellent work on the project!
entry.summary: 19th edition of the European Conference on Logics in Artificial Intelligence

entry.title: Best Paper Award for My Student at CP

link.title: Best Paper Award for My Student at CP

entry.content:
I was very happy to learn, that the paper Symmetric Core Learning for Pseudo-Boolean Optimization by Implicit Hitting Sets by my student Hannes Ihalainen will be awarded the best student paper of the 31st International Conference on Principles and Practice of Constraint Programming, one of the foremost international conference in my research field.

The paper presents an approach for using the symmetries of an optimization problem in order to speed up search for an optimal solution. The paper summarizes work that was started briefly after my 2020 paper on abstract cores when Bart Bogaerts, one of the co-authors of this paper contacted me.

I would like to congratulate Hannes and thank all of the other people on this paper as well, Bart Boagerts and Matti Järvisalo. I look forward to travelling to Glasgow in August and meeting many colleagues and friends.
entry.summary: The 31st International Conference on Principles and Practice of Constraint Programming

entry.title: Disc Golf in Estonia
entry.content:
Last weekend, I went on a trip to Estonia with two of my friends. The aim was to explore the top-rated disc golf courses of Estonia, focusing on courses near Tartu (seeing as the European Disc Golf Festival 2025 was going on in Tallinn).

We are all amateurs, so the primary goal of the trip was to have fun and explore some nice courses. From that perspective, the trip was a huge success. We were delighted with the Hektor Design Hostel in Tartu, with the nearby restaurants, and the courses we played. The only thing that could have been–slightly–better was the weather, which was either a bit hot for achieving maximal performance on the course, or a bit rainy. But on the whole, a very lovely trip. Thanks to Lasse and Tobbe for organizing and being good company.

My travel companions, both of whom are better at disc golf than me.
